6.5.cause: Before: about 10 us of CPU per materials mesh per frame (1,000 boxes), not the video upload. 6.6.cause: Before: about 15 us of CPU per materials mesh per frame (1,000 boxes), not the canvas upload. Fixed by the materials draw-path work through b89ac9c1, with no change of its own; rerun 20261026-165034 shows 0.34 ms CPU against three-webgpu 1.98

8.2.cause: LocalShadows drew all 1,001 casters into each of the 24 cube faces (24,000 draws a frame) and wrote every caster block each frame; casters now draw only into maps whose frustum their bounding sphere reaches and write their block only when moved. Audit (2026-10-26): the world radius took the longest column of the node matrix, short under shear (a rotated child of a non-uniformly scaled parent), so such a caster near a face edge or the light range could lose its shadow in that face; it now uses a bound that holds under shear, plus a float32 pad (shared/sphere.js, tested against sampled sphere points for seams, corners, grazing and sheared casters); the p-point-shadows image is unchanged

fixes.tradeoff: a sphere test per caster per map; casters without bounds (instanced, displaced, or external primitives that give none) still draw into every map

9.1.cause: Uploading a Float32Array as rgba16float converted it with Uint16Array.from(data, toHalf), a callback per value (160 ms for this image in Node). Now the built-in Float16Array bulk conversion (same bits), else a plain loop: 150 -> 16.95 ms against three-webgpu 20.3

fixes.tradeoff: none; bit-identical texels

9.2.cause: The same half-float upload as 9.1, plus parseEXR computing halfToFloat (a 2 ** n) per texel and unpredicting ZIP chunks in three passes. Now a 65,536-entry half table and a one-pass unpredict: 221 -> 19.6 ms against three-webgpu 25.9

fixes.tradeoff: a 256 KiB table, built on the first HALF decode; bit-identical floats

10.11.cause: Before: JS arrays grown by push in the STL read and weld (63 ms in Node) and a fingerprint of the lone part with nothing to match (40 ms): 111 -> 28.7 ms. Then a like-for-like reader: p-stl now times the plain parseSTL (typed arrays, no weld, flat normals computed where the file stores zero): 4.9 ms against three's 2.8, the rest being those computed normals. ACCEPTED difference in work (Scott, 2026-10-26): parseSTL returns a render-ready mesh, while three's STLLoader copies the file's zero normals, which light wrongly until computeVertexNormals() runs; p-stl-normals times that full job (three 8.7 ms, parseSTL 4.7 ms, faster). The old weld-and-parts path (29.4 ms, no three.js equivalent) was measured in its own scene until that scene was removed (2026-10-29).

fixes.tradeoff: worst-case typed arrays, about 260 bytes per triangle while parsing, freed after
+1.9 KB gzip on the loaders root entry (separate module); computes flat normals where the file stores zero

11.3.cause: Before: num() tried toPrecision(1..9) for every number (75% of the time) and CRC-32 ran a byte at a time. Now a binary search with a value cache and slicing-by-8: 52.8 -> 16.0 ms, byte-identical archive. The rest is different output: Margo writes every mesh in world space (2.46 MB for 1,000 boxes), three's archive is 444 KB, so it writes far fewer numbers. Closing it means writing a shared mesh once with per-node transforms, an exporter format change left for a decision

fixes.tradeoff: +500 B gzip on exporters/usdz

12.5.cause: 100 morphed copies each began a render pass and a compute pass, and every draw rebuilt its shader text each frame; models now draw as one run and the shader text steps are memoised. Then the compute pass held 200 dispatches (2 primitives x 100 copies, 150,000 vertices), each writing its own output buffer and run one after another (1.18 ms GPU); every deformed primitive of a device now shares a few buffers and deforms in one dispatch per buffer page and pipeline (2 here): GPU 1.31 -> 0.19 ms, the deformed vertices bit for bit those of the per-primitive path. What is left on the GPU (timestamps per pass, run 20261027-032923): the draw pass takes 0.14 ms against three.js WebGL's whole 0.15 ms frame, which morphs inside its vertex shader; the 0.05 ms deform pass is an ACCEPTED difference in work: Margo deforms each vertex (position, normal, tangent) once a frame into a buffer that every reader shares (gltf-pro draws, shadow casters, TAA velocity, selection outlines, picking and its CPU readback), where three repeats the morph in every pass that draws the mesh and has no deformed geometry to pick or read back. Still slower on CPU: 0.52 against 0.27 ms; measured (browser CPU profile, 5,000 frames): about 55% is gltf-pro re-deriving each of the 200 draws every frame (two-primitive models never join a run, and plain glTF materials have no steady path), about a fifth the Animations' own work; a loss to fix, plan in known-bugs. First frame (run 20261027-103915): 304 ms against three-webgpu 294 and three-webgl 37; every cloneModel copy kept its own mip pipelines (200 shader modules for 100 copies, found with the harness dump); they are now made once per device. The rest of that first frame is WebGPU pipeline compilation and texture upload that the per-primitive path did during the build (build 490 -> 206 ms), open in known-bugs First frame (entry 49 of perf-history.md): every cloneModel copy uploaded and mipped its own textures, 700 textures queued during the build; copies now share one texture per image, so the first frame fell from 249 to 133-187 ms and the build from 177 to 61-76 (busy machine, not gated), the same pixels byte for byte. Render pipeline (entry 56 of perf-history.md): PBRModel.compile() moves its compile into the build; p-morph-compiled's first frame is 17 ms and its build 108-126, 11 to 29 ms less in total than p-morph (busy machine, not gated).

fixes.tradeoff: models share a run only when their passes were added back to back; others draw alone as before
+2.8 KB gzip on the animation root entry (the shared-buffer arena and its WGSL); buffers grow geometrically and are compacted on growth, so a page can hold freed space until then
mip pipelines live as long as the device
a copy cannot hold a texture apart from its source; textures and images live until their last holder goes

fixes.commit: perf(gltf-pro): PBRModel.compile builds render pipelines during the build
fixes.tradeoff: opt-in: the first frame gets shorter and the build longer; only the overlap is saved

12.6.cause: Skeleton.index was a linear name search run per track per call (quadratic in bones); every setPose built its error labels and every track a pose object and a sample array

fixes.tradeoff: none; a clip keeps one bone binding per skeleton it has posed (weakly held)

12.7.cause: every cloneModel copy repacked its vertices (now shared per asset), core Engine.remove scanned every slot of the parent column for each removed mesh (now each mesh keeps its children), and every copy uploaded its own vertex and index buffers, re-baked its static parts and made a view and sampler per map slot (now counted per asset, reused and cached). Still slower (CPU profile): installBatches runs two engine-wide kernel ticks per model, quadratic in the copies (about 6.5 of 17.6 ms), then per-copy uniforms and bind groups and core node creation; three clones on the CPU only

fixes.tradeoff: packed arrays live as long as the asset
a Set of child ids per mesh with children
a model rewrites a geometry buffer in place only while no other copy holds it; the first edit of a shared one uploads a new buffer

13.7.cause: the velocity pass began a render pass per mesh (and a compute pass per PBR snapshot) and rewrote every mesh block each frame because the camera rows were in it; now one render pass, one snapshot pass and one camera block a frame. The image differs from three.js as before (different TAA algorithms; three-webgl has no moving-camera TAA)

fixes.tradeoff: none

16.2.cause: core GPURenderer.pick compiled a shader module and pipeline on every call and rewrote every instance (960 KB for 10,000 boxes); both fixed. Still slower, measured (CPU profile: 0.15 ms of JS a pick, the main thread idle the rest): each pick waits for its own GPU pass and mapAsync readback, about 3.1 ms here, and engine.pick answers overlapping calls one at a time by contract (each reads the scene when its turn comes). three's WebGL readRenderTargetPixels is a synchronous readPixels; three's WebGPU readback is slower than Margo's (423 ms)

fixes.tradeoff: pick pipelines count toward the 64 cached shader variants

17.11.cause: the scene's density function summed every ball at every grid point (4.2 M terms a frame; three writes each ball only near it), and marchingCubes allocated its grids and a 1.8 M-slot vertex table every call. 4be0e7d2 fixed the extractor and also changed the scene to write each ball only near it, so the old p-marching-cubes row compares two workloads (kept as history). The row now runs both, labelled: p-marching-cubes-dense is the original scene with identical maths (its image is byte-identical to the original's), 9.76 ms CPU against three's 3.17, a published loss in work, since three's add-on never sums every ball everywhere; p-marching-cubes-localized does the add-on's work, 2.90 against 3.17 (run 20261026-221004, image SSIM 0.9986 against the dense one: normals from the grid gradient). Rerun both with `node bench/cli.mjs parity --cases=p-marching-cubes --engines=margo,three-webgpu-parity,three-webgl-parity --runs=5 --warmup=1 --no-compare --no-fail`

fixes.tradeoff: marchingCubes takes a sampled grid (normals from the grid gradient instead of the function's); 816 more gzip bytes in procedural

9.3.cause: p-pmrem (run 20261027-105122): 14.6 -> 10.9 ms against three-webgl's 5.0. Environment.create converted the 1024 x 512 HDR to half floats with a bit-twiddling loop each call (7.4 ms in Node); it now stores through the built-in Float16Array (same bits, about 3x faster). What is left (browser CPU profile: 70% of the call idle, waiting for the GPU and the readback) is work three's PMREMGenerator does not do: Margo also uploads the equirect each call, builds a source cube with its mip chain, computes L2 SH irradiance and reads it back to the CPU (a GPU round trip), and computes a 128 x 128 BRDF LUT (512 samples a texel) per environment; three's timed call reuses its uploaded texture and computes only the specular levels. Open: the BRDF LUT does not depend on the image and can be shared per device (known-bugs). helmet, measured (timestamps per pass with each feature switched off): IBL costs nothing measurable; Margo's default shadow filter, PCSS ('soft': 16 blocker reads and 32 comparison taps per lit pixel, spread over a penumbra up to a tenth of the map), is 0.68 of helmet's 0.78 ms GPU, where three's side draws one PCFSoftShadowMap. With the closest setup (helmet-filterpcf-cascades1: filter 'pcf', 1 cascade) Margo draws in 0.08 ms GPU against three's WebGL 0.09 and WebGPU 0.07, the same image (SSIM 0.984); still slower on CPU, 0.11 against 0.07 ms (CPU profile: spread over the frame's four passes, shadow map, core meshes, the model and the MSAA resolve, with core's render the largest share)

fixes.tradeoff: none; bit-identical half floats

11.4.cause: encodeEXR yielded to the event loop every 65,536 samples with setTimeout, which a browser clamps to 4 ms once nested: 128 yields for this 2048 x 1024 RGBA image, about 0.5 s of timers against about 0.05 s of encoding (680 ms against three-webgl's 223). It now yields after about 10 ms of encoding (scheduler.yield() where the browser has it): 44.6 ms against 154 (run 20261027-104327), byte-identical files. Not a like-for-like win: encodeEXR writes NONE (uncompressed, about twice the bytes), three's EXRExporter ZIP-compresses, so Margo does less work here

fixes.tradeoff: onProgress is called at each yield (about every 10 ms) instead of every 65,536 samples

4.6.cause: Before (Node CPU profile): extrudeGeometry grew JS arrays by push with spread arguments and a new UV array per corner, then copied them (about a fifth), and the triangulator keyed shared edges and pinch points by printing coordinates to strings (cancelSharedEdges, joinHoles: about a third of triangulation). The arrays are now sized up front and written by index, and coordinates are grouped by value (0 and -0 alike, as the strings were). Same bytes (hashes of the text geometry and of 4,000 random touching-ring triangulations unchanged): 23.6 -> 13.4 ms against three-webgl's 8.0 (run 20261027-104327). What is left is the triangulator, about 60% of the call in Node: an ACCEPTED difference in work (rule 12): Margo cuts small, well-shaped ears first (a priority queue with grid ear tests) and survives touching, pinched and self-intersecting rings (Eberly bridges, edge cancellation, FIST-style escalation), where an ear-cutting fast path takes the first ear it finds; no like-for-like row exists, because Margo has no lower-quality triangulator to time

fixes.commit: perf(geometry): extrude in place, coordinate groups
fixes.tradeoff: +376 B gzip on geometry/extrude (the coordinate grouping)

10.8.cause: Before (Node and browser CPU profiles): about 40% of parseFBX was the FBX pivot chain, 11 matrices composed per node per animation key, each step allocating a new matrix (and identity matrices built from array literals), with the fixed parts (pivots, offsets, pre- and post-rotation) rebuilt every key. Those parts are now made once per node and the product runs through scratch matrices, the same multiplications in the same order (byte-identical GLB): 12.6 -> 5.8 ms against three-webgl's 4.7 (run 20261027-105122). Still slower: parseFBX converts FBX to an in-memory GLB and parses that with gltf-pro (validation, the glTF material model), where three builds its objects directly

fixes.commit: perf(fbx): pivot chain once per node
fixes.tradeoff: a cached pivot chain per FBX node while converting

10.1.cause: Before: every image was decoded one after another (each createImageBitmap awaited before the next began), so the call paid the sum of FlightHelmet's decodes, and each image's bytes were copied once more before the Blob. Browser images now decode up to 8 at once, in image order (the size limits stop at the same image; KTX2 stays one at a time), without the extra copy: 88.7 -> 46.3 ms against three-webgl's 34.0 (run 20261027-105432). Left (CPU profile): native decode and upload work and accessor validation (finite checks on every value), plus closing the previous call's bitmaps inside the timing

fixes.tradeoff: up to 7 decoded images more in memory at once while a model loads; +1.7 KB gzip on gltf-pro/worker

2.5.cause: 10,000 RawMeshes of one material, one draw each. Before: each mesh's frame rebuilt its normal matrix with temporary arrays and re-bound the material's group (CPU profile). Now the object block is recomputed only when the world matrix changed and the material group is bound once per run of draws: 28.8 -> 21.3 ms CPU (run 20261027-105724) against three-webgpu's 36.8 and three-webgl's 7.6. Left (measured with a timing wrapper on the pass methods): the native encoding calls themselves, per mesh a bind group (its own object block), a vertex buffer, an index buffer and an indexed draw, about 1.7 us of every 2.1 us a mesh; three's WebGL backend issues cheaper GL calls. Structural, plan in known-bugs (shared GPU buffers for identical raw geometry, one pooled object buffer with dynamic offsets)

fixes.commit: perf(shader): raw object blocks and material group
fixes.tradeoff: none; the same draws and buffer writes

Run 20261027-103915 (busy machine): CPU 17.5 ms against three-webgl's 13.3 and three-webgpu's 22.9

fixes.commit: perf(animation): comparisons stop at the first change
